h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: A conv on the direct input-to-output edge looks like pure added capacity, but parents that already have a strong conv path gain little and may lose the cheap residual path.
One might think feeding a strong edge 5 makes conv on edge 1 more useful, but headroom means strong parents improve less from any helpful edit.
Deepening the node-1 path seems to matter more when edge 4 carries a conv, but parents with a conv on edge 4 are already strong and have less headroom.
One might think removing an edge hurts strong parents more, but a parallel 3x3 conv into node 3 makes edge 5 redundant, so removing it costs less.
A residual skip might seem to cushion a weak pooling edge, but parents with a skip on edge 3 are strong, and harmful edits do more damage when there is more to lose.
Shallow cells might seem not to need a residual path, but removing the skip on edge 3 drops a key feature of top cells, whereas removing other ops on edge 3 is often neutral.
Pooling might seem harmless when node 1 already supplies conv features, but parents with a conv on edge 0 are strong, and harmful edits hurt more there.
Adding a conv anywhere seems to help, but parents that already have a 3x3 conv on edge 5 have less headroom, so a 1x1 conv on edge 0 helps less.
A 1x1 conv looks like a near-equivalent swap, but replacing the strongest op is a net loss while replacing weaker ops is roughly neutral or a gain.
Stacking convs into node 2 looks like it should compound, but a second 3x3 conv into the same node shows diminishing returns.
